## The prose

10:12 a.m., March 3 — moved in.

I had parked the last box under the threadbare wardrobe and stood for a long minute in the doorway because 67 Fairfax folded around me like an old hand: the constant, faint smell of boiled tea and old paper, the stairs that complained in a different key with each step, and the thin walls that let the hall sound through as if it belonged to my room too. Mrs. Hollis met me on the landing with a key on a neat ribbon looped over one finger, small and exact as the woman who owned it.

She was exactly as you'd expect from her photographs in other people's mouths: small, precise, habit-bound. She inclined her head once, clipped the name from my lips, and ticked off rules in sentences that behaved like lists.

"No smoking in the house, please. No late visitors up past eleven. And don't be troubled by the hall clock — it's been stopped since before my time; there's nothing to be done about it."

It was the way she said it — the civility with an edge of practised reluctance — that made me ask, before I could be polite, whether we'd met before. "No," she said, with a quick, patient smile that folded thought away. "This is the first proper time."

11:03 a.m. — I wrote the hour in my notebook as habit demanded, because writing things down made them smaller, manageable. Mrs. Hollis showed me where I could put the kettle and pointed at the hallway with the same clipped hand: "Don't worry about it; the clock's stopped at 4:22, it likes that time."

I noted the stopped face of the broken clock as she mentioned it and then shut the door on the landing's soft light. My room was smaller than I expected: a single bed, a narrow wardrobe, a wall-hung mirror with a hairline crack low on its glass, and a strip of floral wallpaper behind the wardrobe where someone had made a patch.

The patch was fresher than the rest of the wall: its edge had the clean, un-aged line of a recent glue job. Behind the wardrobe, in the right-hand corner where the paper had been tucked and folded by a careful thumb, there was a narrow gap beneath the lining.

I shifted the wardrobe and my fingers went into that seam without thinking. It gave like a mouth and something small and silver slid against my knuckle — cold with dust.

11:07 a.m. — found silver locket.

The locket was dented on one side, its chain run through with the almost-absence of a loop. A smear ran along the rim, red-brown in the way rust leans and dark like dried mud, so I turned it over on the palm of my hand as if it might explain itself. The silver and the way it had been dented looked almost a century old — early twentieth century; the metal was worn thin at the edges in a way the chain, barely there, did not match.

When I prised it open the photograph inside was a faded sepia: a child with a broken toy held in both hands, the edges curled and soft. On the reverse, two letters had been scratched clumsily into the silver — E.L. — shallow enough that dust sat in the grooves. The whole piece smelled faintly of old soap and a hint of lavender; a scatter of powder dusted the hinge.

I held the locket up to the mirror. The hairline crack distorted the lower third of the reflection so the dented edge of the locket seemed doubled, as if two small mouths were making a secret of the photograph between them.

I slipped the locket into my pocket and, without thinking, wrote a quick line in my notebook: "11:07 — silver locket. E.L."

11:07 a.m. — silver locket. E.L.

2:00 a.m. — footsteps above.
3:12 a.m. — footsteps above.

I had written both times down the way I always did, as if ink could fix an angle of the world. The footsteps came like a small clock: a measured pair of thuds, pause, another pair. They had woken me twice in the week since I moved in, and each time I had checked my watch and put the minute beside the note in my notebook. There was nothing cinematic about them; they carried through the house the way the hall sounds had in the morning — thin joists, hollow cavities, a precise resonance that translated attic wood into something you felt under the pillow.

The next morning I climbed up the narrow ladder to the attic with a torch and my notebook in my breast pocket. 9:14 a.m. — attic. Cold light came through the gable and the whole place smelled of dust and old varnish. The trapdoor had a crescent of white on the hinge: damp chalk smudges, the chalk itself soft to the touch as if it had been pressed and rubbed minutes, not years, ago. A jar on a low crate wore pale handprints around its rim where someone had held it; the powder on the prints still felt faintly tacky when I brushed at it with a fingertip.

I moved a tea tin that had been balanced like an afterthought on the central joist and there, under its dented lid, the doll lay on its side. 9:21 a.m. — porcelain doll. It had one glass eye gone; the socket stared with an empty glaze. A braided ribbon was knotted to its wrist and a smear of dried mud darkened the hem of its dress. The doll smelled like attic dust and something faintly of garden earth. I set it on my palm and its small porcelain head swung as if someone had just breathed near it.

Along the northern eaves I found the diary wedged tight under a beam where the rafters met the floor. 9:26 a.m. — diary and drawing. The cloth cover was frayed and the handwriting was small, earnest and a little slanted. Short entries, dates in a child’s hand; one page had a drawing of a toy with a bent wheel that looked, at a glance, like the broken toy in the photograph I had opened in the locket. At the back a page had been torn out and the torn corner folded back into the lining like a secret.

Three boards from the trapdoor the floor was slightly springy. I levered the loose plank and the edge came up with a greyed sigh. 9:33 a.m. — floorboard plank. The cavity beneath held a narrow bundle of papers and envelopes the size of a child's palm; beneath them the subfloor bore a dark, stubborn stain. The stain was dry when I touched it — a dark patch that smelled faintly of iron and old cloth, as if something had bled and then been left to the dust. I photographed it quickly with my phone and wrote the time down.

Everything in that attic behaved like evidence. The chalk at the trapdoor hinge was damp; the jar had thumbprints in white powder; the joists carried the exact cadence of footfalls into the bedroom below. Nothing looked staged, nothing supernatural in the theatrical sense — only small, repeatable marks that a child might have made and, for reasons that did not yet make sense, continued to make.

I sat on the floor with the doll in one hand and the diary open on my knees, the locket warm against my palm where I had taken it out to compare the bent wheel in the drawing to the photograph inside it. The bent toy in the picture and the child's scrawl in the diary matched close enough that I could not dismiss the likeness. And the smear along the locket's rim stayed unexplained, a dark comma I had not yet read.

9:48 a.m. — I wrote the time and the feeling: a small presence, patient and precise, and an anxiety that had the shape of a clock hand moving steadily toward something I could not yet name.

## The prose

11:11 a.m. — as before, I wrote the time because habit made facts easier to hold. I set my phone on the narrow mantel, opened the recorder and left it facing the stairs. The file named itself: 2026-03-03_11-11-00_mantel_record.wav. I stuck a sticky note beside the broken clock with the time on it and took the two photographs I'd planned: one straight on to capture the stopped hands, one oblique to show the hairline dent along the rim.

11:18 a.m. — the hands sat at four twenty-two. The photograph saved as 2026-03-03_clock_4-22_front.jpg. It was not a theatrical stop; it simply sat with its hands like folded palms.

11:27 a.m. — in my bedroom I propped the sepia photograph against the cracked mirror and let raking light coax the back into view. The ink was faint and smeared; under the light the letters resolved. On my phone screen it read, as legible as the smear allowed, "Oct 12 1913." I photographed the back again and labelled the file 2026-03-03_sepia_back_rakinglight.jpg.

11:34 a.m. — I laid the locket beside the diary page I'd photographed in the attic and took close-ups. The letters on the silver were shallow and crude; in my photographs the inscription appeared to read E.L. I compared the capital E in the diary photograph with the E on the locket until the shapes stopped feeling accidental. The loop of the capital, the slant of the lower-case l — they matched closely enough that I could not set the thought down. I made a cautious note in my notebook, as I always did: "11:07 — silver locket. E.L." That earlier line sat on the page like a stitch I could follow back.

11:44 a.m. — I returned to the attic with a ruler and a north marker and photographed the dark patch beneath the loose plank again. In the light the stain read the colour of old tea — a bruised brown with speckled edges and a dry, stubborn skin. I took a macro and the file saved as 2026-03-03_stain_under_plank_macro.jpg.

I sat on a joist and read the torn fragment aloud, careful to say it exactly as it lay: "—spilt tea under the boards. Don't tell." Those four words fit like a key and the rest of the page fell into a context I could map: "Oct 12 — tea and the clock. The clock stopped at four and twenty-two when Mam went for sugar." I read the fragment again until the letters were not suggestion but fact on the paper in front of me.

Before I climbed down the house made the sound it had been making: two small thuds, a pause, then two more, each set measured and the same. The recorder on the mantel showed distinct ticks at two predictable hours later that night; what I had seen in the attic read as the same small repertoire — an anchored, repetitive motion across the joists rather than anything wild.

12:05 p.m. — Mrs. Hollis stood at the sink in the kitchen with her hands folded around a chipped mug. I put the photograph of the locket and the torn page between us and tapped the back of the sepia. "It reads, faintly, 'Oct 12 1913'," I said, and then, more cautiously, "the inscription on the locket appears to be E.L., and the diary fragment says, verbatim, '—spilt tea under the boards. Don't tell.' The stain under the plank looks like old tea." She folded her hands tighter and let a patience smooth her face.

"Children left long ago," she said, clipped. Her fingers found a jar of preserves and slid it to the side like a small shield. "This house has its ways. We don't keep much past what's necessary." She did not deny the paper; she did not offer an explanation.

12:17 p.m. — I wrote the new observations into my notebook the way habit had taught me, the same habit that had me write "11:07 — silver locket. E.L." earlier. I noted the sepia's faint, smeared ink reading as "Oct 12 1913," the locket's inscription as appearing E.L., and I copied the torn fragment exactly: "—spilt tea under the boards. Don't tell." The connections were small and physical — paper, ink, a bruise-brown stain under a board and the same slant of an E — and that made them sharper than any theory. I closed the notebook on the smell of old tea and the steady pair of footfalls that the house would not, for now, stop making.

## The prose

I set the torn page, the locket and the close-up of the stain on the kitchen table and waited for the house to say its piece. Mrs. Hollis sat opposite me with a chipped mug between her palms, small movements that kept her calm. Above us the ceiling answered with the familiar two thuds, a pause, two more — the child's cadence like a watch that would not stop.

"Read it again," I said. The paper felt thin and conciliatory between my fingers. I read, careful not to smudge the ragged edge: "—spilt tea under the boards. Don't tell."

Something whispered it back in a voice that had the size and cadence of a child: "Don't tell."

Mrs. Hollis folded her hands and did not look away. The civility on her face thinned; the practiced patience rearranged itself into something brittle. When she spoke, she chose simple shapes instead of a speech.

"Her name was Elsie L.," she said. "The photograph's date — October the twelfth, 1913." She set her jaw and her fingers went to the hem of her skirt. "I wasn't thinking straight. I went across the kitchen for a jar of sugar; while I was gone she had an accident. I hid her and I told people she had been sent away."

I tilted the locket under the lamp. The shallow letters on the silver caught the light: E.L., rubbed and honest. Beside it the sepia's smear resolved into the same date I had coaxed from the back of the photograph. The pieces fitted with the cold logic of things that do not need imagination.

I said nothing more. Evidence does the work better than an accusation, so I took her by the sleeve and we climbed the narrow ladder together.

The plank gave with a soft, greyed sigh. Beneath the bundle of child's papers the subfloor showed a dark, circular mark: tannin-brown, the colour of over‑steeped tea, its edges specked with dust and a tacky, glue-like ring around the rim where something had been bound fast. I scraped at that rim with my thumbnail; a powder came away like an apology.

I held up the porcelain doll. The ribbon braided at its wrist matched the loop the diary's folded page suggested: a child had tied something on purpose. The diary itself mentioned fastening a ribbon to the doll so it would remember. The alignment of that sentence and the physical braid was too clean to shrug off.

When I set the doll on the joist it moved, not with the theatrics of a story but with a single, practicable push. It slid sideways, nudged at the air and came to rest in my palm as if a small hand had placed it there.

On the attic hatch, fresh white strokes formed the single, wobbly letter of a child's name: an E. I hadn't made it. Chalk dust feathered the strokes. The voice that followed did its small, circling thing: "Don't tell."

The measured footfalls that had occupied the house stopped as if someone had wound down a watch. The silence was immediate and the house seemed to sit back, listening.

Mrs. Hollis's shoulders finally let go of their posture. "I was frightened," she said, voice cracked and ordinary. "I sealed that space myself the same day. I thought saying she was sent away would keep the questions away. I thought I was saving the house from scandal, and I wound up keeping a child from being spoken for." Her hands trembled where they had rested on the ladder.

In the cracked mirror on the landing my reflection showed me holding the dented locket; the dent caught the light like a pinprick. Beside my face the mirror held a thin absence — not a shape but the memory of one — where a child's voice had been. I felt the house exhale. For the first time since I moved in, the small, clockwork sounds that answered me stopped moving at all.
